title: No Other Gospel
subtitle: Galatians 1:1–10
description: Paul opens with credentials instead of thanksgiving, and curses any gospel but the one first preached.
paragraphs: The churches of Galatia were brand new when this letter reached them. They were the converts of Paul's first journey, the crowds who had heard him in Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe and believed, Jews and God-fearing Gentiles together, circumcised and uncircumcised at one table. After Paul moved on, teachers arrived behind him with a correction: faith in Jesus was a beginning, but full membership in God's people required circumcision and the law of Moses. Word of it reached Paul, and he wrote back at white heat. Whether he wrote just before the Jerusalem council took up this exact question, or some years after it, the letter itself does not say, and honest readers disagree; what is certain is that this is the argument the council had to answer. Readers who know Paul's other letters will feel the difference in the first lines. There is no thanksgiving section, no prayer for the readers' growth, none of the warmth he usually opens with. He begins with his credentials, because his credentials are what the new teachers have been shredding.

“Paul, an apostle,” the letter starts, and immediately the defense: he is “sent not from men nor by man, but by Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised Him from the dead.” The men with him send greetings too, but the greeting itself is the whole gospel in miniature. “Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ,” and then, before any request or rebuke, the cross stated as a rescue: Christ “gave Himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father.” The glory goes to God “forever and ever. Amen.” No human being is thanked in this opening, which is the point. If God the Father and the risen Christ are the senders, and the Father's will is the plan, then a gospel amended by later arrivals in Galatia answers to a higher court than theirs.

Then the warmth that is missing turns out to have been spent on astonishment. “I am amazed,” Paul writes, “how quickly you are deserting the One who called you by the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel.” Not deserting Paul; deserting God, the One who called them. And the rival message is denied the name it claims: it is a gospel “which is not even a gospel.” Behind the Galatians' confusion stand identifiable operators, and Paul names their trade without naming them: “some people are troubling you and trying to distort the gospel of Christ.” Troubling is a word for unsettling a community's peace, and distort is a craftsman's word, to twist a thing out of its true shape. Paul's charge is not that the new teachers preach a harsher religion, but that they have bent the one gospel until it points at the Galatians' own performance instead of at the cross.

What follows is the most solemn sentence Paul ever wrote, written twice. “But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be under a curse!” The witnesses he imagines against himself are ranked deliberately: his own team first, then a messenger from heaven itself. No authority outranks the message once delivered, not even the deliverer's. Then he repeats it word for word, with a note that this is a repetition: “As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be under a curse!” The Galatians had evidently heard this standard from Paul in person, on the ground, before any rival arrived. The letter is not introducing a new severity. It is reminding them of the test they were given at the start, and asking them to apply it now, to the smooth and confident men who followed him.

The chapter closes with the accusation underneath all the others, answered in three questions. The teachers' working charge against Paul was evidently that his law-free gospel was a sales pitch, a message tailored to please hearers by asking little of them. “Am I now seeking the approval of men, or of God? Or am I striving to please men?” Paul asks. “If I were still trying to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ.” Still is the loaded word: there was a time when pleasing men was his profession, and the Galatians have heard that story. A man currying favor does not open a letter with a double curse, does not tell new converts they are deserting God, does not stake everything on a message his hearers find offensive. The defense that follows will not be a theory. It will be the biography itself, the gospel's origin in a persecutor's ruined career, produced as evidence. But the letter's logic is already whole in its first page: there is one gospel, it came from God, and anybody who amends it, even an angel, is to be refused.

title: The Gospel I Received
subtitle: Galatians 1:11–24
description: Paul’s gospel did not come from men: a ruined career, a desert, and fifteen days in Jerusalem, sworn to.
paragraphs: Paul's defense begins with the origin of his message, because that is the point the rival teachers could not afford to grant him. If his gospel came from Jerusalem, Jerusalem could amend it. If it came from men at all, men could improve on it. So he states the negative twice and the positive once: “the gospel I preached was not devised by man.” “I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it; rather, I received it by revelation from Jesus Christ.” Everything else in this chapter is evidence for that one claim, and the evidence is a life story the Galatians had already heard once from his own mouth. He is not informing them. He is putting them back in the witness box: you have heard this before; now judge what the new men are asking you to forget.

The first exhibit is the career the gospel destroyed. You have heard of my former way of life in Judaism, he writes: “how severely I persecuted the church of God and tried to destroy it.” He was not a seeker drifting toward a softer faith. “I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries and was extremely zealous for the traditions of my fathers.” Advancing is a career word, and the career was brilliant: the traditions guarded, the church hunted, the future assured. A gospel invented by such a man would have protected that investment. The one he received liquidated it, turned the persecutor into the persecuted, and made his name a scandal to the very people whose approval the Galatian teachers now say he craves. Whatever else the revelation on the Damascus road was, it was not a business decision.

The call itself is told in God's verbs, not Paul's. “But when God, who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me by His grace, was pleased to reveal His Son in me so that I might preach Him among the Gentiles,” then Paul's response was deliberately small: “I did not rush to consult with flesh and blood.” No trip to Jerusalem for certification, no apprenticeship under the apostles who came before him. “I went into Arabia and later returned to Damascus.” The years that should embarrass his claim, the years with no Jerusalem contact at all, are the years he exhibits as proof. A gospel learned from men requires men in the story. Paul's story has a desert where the classroom should be.

When the Jerusalem visit finally comes, he timestamps and measures it like a man filing an affidavit. “Only after three years did I go up to Jerusalem to confer with Cephas, and I stayed with him fifteen days.” Fifteen days, one apostle and one other: “I saw none of the other apostles except James, the Lord’s brother.” Then the sentence that turns biography into testimony under oath: “I assure you before God that what I am writing to you is no lie.” Paul swears because he knows what is at stake in the arithmetic. Three years of independence, a fortnight's visit, two men seen. The teachers' version needs Paul formed, briefed, and sent by Jerusalem. His own ledger has no room in it for their story.

After that visit he disappears from the capital's records for years: “Later I went to the regions of Syria and Cilicia.” And the Judean churches, the very heartland of the faith, knew him only by a rumor running ahead of him: “I was personally unknown, however, to the churches of Judea that are in Christ. They only heard the account: ‘The man who formerly persecuted us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.’ And they glorified God because of me.” Luke's Acts, it should be said plainly, shows Paul in Jerusalem more often across these years than this letter counts, and the two records were never reconciled by their authors. The letter's argument does not need Acts' itinerary; it needs only this, and on this Paul has sworn: the gospel he preaches to Gentiles was not handed to him by the men the Galatians are now being told to obey. The revelation made him, and the next fourteen years, when he finally lays them before Jerusalem, will test whether the men there find anything in it to add.

title: The Right Hand of Fellowship
subtitle: Galatians 2:1–14
description: Jerusalem adds nothing and takes Titus uncircumcised; then Peter’s table at Antioch breaks the fellowship.
paragraphs: “Fourteen years later I went up again to Jerusalem, accompanied by Barnabas. I took Titus along also.” The trip was not a summons. “I went in response to a revelation and set before them the gospel that I preach among the Gentiles.” Paul laid his life's work on the table in a private session with the recognized leaders, and he gives the reason without embarrassment: he spoke to them “for fear that I was running or had already run in vain.” Not fear that his gospel was wrong, but fear of a fracture, a race run in two directions by men preaching one Christ. Whether this visit is the famine relief trip Luke records in Acts 11 or the council of Acts 15, Paul does not say, and this telling will not decide it for him. What matters to his argument is what Jerusalem did when it heard the gospel whole: it added nothing, and it tested it on a Greek.

Titus was the test case standing in the room. “Yet not even Titus, who was with me, was compelled to be circumcised, even though he was a Greek.” The pressure to circumcise him was real, and Paul traces it to infiltrators: the issue “arose because some false brothers had come in under false pretenses to spy on our freedom in Christ Jesus, in order to enslave us.” Spy and enslave are military words, and the answer matches them: “We did not give in to them for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel would remain with you.” Remain with you is addressed to the Galatians themselves. The stand taken over one Greek's body in Jerusalem is the reason a church hundreds of miles away can still hear the gospel unamended, and Paul wants them to feel the debt before he asks them not to surrender what it bought.

Then comes the sentence the rival teachers could not survive. The leaders, the men of reputation, examined the gospel Paul preached among the Gentiles, and “those leaders added nothing to me.” His aside about their reputation is almost rude: “whatever they were makes no difference to me; God does not show favoritism.” What the pillars saw, instead of a deficiency to correct, was a commission parallel to Peter's own: “they saw that I had been entrusted to preach the gospel to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been to the circumcised.” One gospel, two fields, and the same God working both: “the One who was at work in Peter’s apostleship to the circumcised was also at work in my apostleship to the Gentiles.”

So the meeting ended in partnership, not probation. Recognizing the grace given to Paul, James, Cephas, and John, the reputed pillars, “gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, so that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcised.” One condition only was attached, and it was not circumcision: “They only asked us to remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do.” The right hand is the letter's high-water mark of unity, and it is placed here deliberately, because the next scene tests whether the fellowship survives contact with a dinner table.

At Antioch it did not, and the man who failed was Peter himself. “When Cephas came to Antioch, however, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned.” Peter had been eating with Gentile believers freely. “For before certain men came from James, he used to eat with the Gentiles.” Then the delegation arrived. “But when they arrived, he began to draw back and separate himself, for fear of those in the circumcision group.” The withdrawal spread like weather: “The other Jews joined him in his hypocrisy, so that by their hypocrisy even Barnabas was led astray.” Even Barnabas, Paul's own partner, the man who had stood beside him in Jerusalem. Paul's rebuke was public, because the damage was public: “If you, who are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?” A Jew who eats like a Gentile cannot, by withdrawing his table, pressure Gentiles to become Jews to regain his company. Paul never tells the Galatians what Peter answered, or whether he answered at all. The letter leaves the confrontation standing, unrepaired, as its own argument: the gospel's truth is not protected by the reputations of the men who carry it, not even Peter's, and a table divided by fear has already voted on the doctrine, whatever the mouths around it say.

title: Crucified with Christ
subtitle: Galatians 2:15–3:14
description: Justified by faith, not works of law, and Abraham’s blessing reaches the Gentiles through the curse borne on a tree.
paragraphs: Paul's words to Peter at Antioch do not end at the table. They run on into the doctrinal center of the letter, the argument everything else defends. Jews by birth, he says, men who grew up inside the law rather than outside it, “know that a man is not justified by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ.” The conclusion is stated as shared knowledge, not new theory: “So we, too, have believed in Christ Jesus, that we may be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified.” Justified is a courtroom word, declared in the right, and Paul deletes the law from the verdict's grounds for Jew and Gentile alike. The men in Galatia are being told the courtroom still keeps a side door marked works. Paul, who was born in the courtroom, says there is no door.

The objections arrive on schedule, and he answers them like a man who has had this argument in a dozen synagogues. If men justified in Christ keep on sinning, “does that make Christ a minister of sin? Certainly not!” The sin lies in the rebuilding: “If I rebuild what I have already torn down, I prove myself to be a lawbreaker.” The law itself performed the demolition, rightly used: “For through the law I died to the law so that I might live to God.” Then the letter's best-known sentence, spoken not as doctrine in the abstract but as the apostle's own autopsy and address: “I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me. The life I live in the body, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave Himself up for me.” And its corollary, which turns grace into arithmetic: “I do not set aside the grace of God. For if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing.”

With the doctrine standing, Paul wheels on the Galatians' own biography. “O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? Before your very eyes Jesus Christ was clearly portrayed as crucified.” Bewitched is a spell word, half insult, half diagnosis: something has interfered with their eyes. Then the interrogation narrows to one question he demands they answer from memory: “Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law, or by hearing with faith?” They know the answer; they were there. “Are you so foolish? After starting in the Spirit, are you now finishing in the flesh?” The contrast is between the Spirit's beginning and the flesh's finishing school, and Paul presses it into the present tense: “Does God lavish His Spirit on you and work miracles among you because you practice the law, or because you hear and believe?” Their own congregation's life is the exhibit. God had not waited for their circumcision to lavish anything.

The argument then leaves experience for Scripture, and the witness called is Abraham. Paul quotes Genesis the way the Galatians' teachers would have to answer it: “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.” Belief first, credit second, circumcision not yet in the story at all. “Understand, then, that those who have faith are sons of Abraham.” Sonship runs through faith, not through the knife: “The Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, and foretold the gospel to Abraham: ‘All nations will be blessed through you.’ So those who have faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith.” The Gentile believers in Galatia are not late applicants begging admission to Abraham's house through a legal door. In Paul's reading they are the blessing's destination, named in the promise before the law existed.

The other road is priced in the same Scripture. “All who rely on works of the law are under a curse. For it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law.’” The curse is not for breaking this or that command; it is for relying on the whole and doing less than everything, which is every man's biography. And faith and law are different instruments altogether: “The righteous will live by faith,” while the law's own rule runs the other way, “The man who does these things will live by them.” Into that closed account steps the exchange at the letter's center: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. For it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree.’” The cursed place, the cross Paul had portrayed before their eyes, is where the curse was absorbed. The purpose is stated twice over, once for the nations and once for the promise: “He redeemed us in order that the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, so that by faith we might receive the promise of the Spirit.” The Spirit they received by hearing with faith was not a down payment on a law career. He was the inheritance itself, arriving by the road Abraham walked.

title: A Guardian Until Christ
subtitle: Galatians 3:15–4:7
description: The promise predates the law by 430 years; the guardian’s custody ends in adoption and the cry of Abba.
paragraphs: Paul now argues like a lawyer with a dated document. “Brothers, let me put this in human terms. Even a human covenant, once it is ratified, cannot be canceled or amended.” If a man's settled will cannot be rewritten by later parties, God's cannot either, and the covenant in question names its beneficiary with a precision Paul stops to underline: “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. The Scripture does not say, ‘and to seeds,’ meaning many, but ‘and to your seed,’ meaning One, who is Christ.” The chronology then does the heavy work: “The law that came 430 years later does not revoke the covenant previously established by God, so as to nullify the promise.” Four centuries of law cannot amend a promise already ratified, because the two instruments run on different principles: “For if the inheritance depends on the law, then it no longer depends on a promise; but God freely granted it to Abraham through a promise.”

That raises the obvious question, and Paul asks it before the teachers can: if the promise carried everything, “Why then was the law given? It was added because of transgressions, until the arrival of the seed to whom the promise referred.” Added is the load-bearing word: the law is an appendix, not the covenant itself, and it was temporary by design, with an expiry date set at its issue. Even its delivery was secondhand, “administered through angels by a mediator,” where the promise came from God directly; Paul notes the machinery almost in passing, “A mediator is unnecessary, however, for only one party; but God is one,” and moves on before the detail can swallow the argument. The law is no rival to the promise, and he denies the charge flatly: “Is the law, then, opposed to the promises of God? Certainly not!” Its work was confinement, and it did that work on everyone: “the Scripture pronounces all things confined by sin, so that by faith in Jesus Christ the promise might be given to those who believe.”

The confinement has one famous name in this letter. “Before this faith came, we were held in custody under the law, locked up until faith should be revealed. So the law became our guardian to lead us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith.” A guardian in a wealthy household was the slave assigned to a child: escort, supervisor, disciplinarian, necessary and resented in equal measure, and never the heir's permanent condition. The date of discharge is not the child's improvement but faith's arrival: “Now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian.” To return to the law after faith, on Paul's picture, is not maturity. It is a grown heir re-enrolling under his childhood escort.

What replaces the guardian is sonship, stated in a rush of sentences that has carried baptismal water ever since: “You are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus. For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ.” Then the levelling line the Galatian teachers' program could not pronounce: “There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” The pairs are the ancient world's three great divisions, ancestry, station, and sex, and all three are declared irrelevant to standing in the family. The conclusion closes the chapter's circle back to Abraham: “And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed and heirs according to the promise.”

The picture widens into a household in the next breath. “What I am saying is that as long as the heir is a child, he is no different from a slave, although he is the owner of everything. He is subject to guardians and trustees until the date set by his father.” Israel's centuries under the law were the family's minority, and the Galatians shared the condition in their own pagan form: “when we were children, we were enslaved under the basic principles of the world.” Then the date set by the Father arrived: “But when the time had fully come, God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law, that we might receive our adoption as sons.” Adoption is the destination, and its evidence is not a certificate but a voice: “And because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying out, ‘Abba, Father!’” The Aramaic word of a child for his father, on Gentile lips, by the Spirit's own speaking. Paul sums up the whole movement in one sentence addressed to each Galatian singly: “So you are no longer a slave, but a son; and since you are a son, you are also an heir through God.” The teachers are offering sons a return to the nursery, with the guardian's rod. Paul has just spent two chapters proving the nursery is closed.

title: Hagar and Sarah
subtitle: Galatians 4:8–31
description: Paul reads Abraham’s two sons as two covenants, and asks which mother the Galatians mean to claim.
paragraphs: The doctrine finished, Paul turns from the Galatians' creed to their calendar, and his grief sharpens into alarm. They had been pagans once: “Formerly, when you did not know God, you were slaves to those who by nature are not gods.” Now they know God, and the knowing is corrected mid-sentence into something better: “But now that you know God, or rather are known by God, how is it that you are turning back to those weak and worthless principles? Do you wish to be enslaved by them all over again?” The evidence he cites is not circumcision certificates but a diary: “You are observing special days and months and seasons and years!” A church scheduling its holiness is, to Paul, a household of freed slaves measuring out the old chains by the month. His fear lands flat and personal: “I fear for you, that my efforts for you may have been in vain.”

Then the letter does something no systematic treatise would do. It pleads. “I beg you, brothers, become like me, for I became like you. You have done me no wrong.” Paul had lived as a Gentile among them, law-free, and asks them to return the exchange in kind. He reminds them how the relationship began, in weakness neither side chose: “You know that it was because of an illness that I first preached the gospel to you.” The detour that stranded him in Galatia had put a sick man at their mercy, and their answer had been honor: “you did not despise or reject me. Instead, you welcomed me as if I were an angel of God, as if I were Christ Jesus Himself.” His testimony to their love reaches for the most extravagant fact available: “if it were possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me.” Whatever the illness was, and the letter never names it, the Galatians had loved the afflicted messenger past reason. Now they are cool toward the healthy argument, and he asks the question the whole appeal turns on: “Have I now become your enemy by telling you the truth?”

The rivals, meanwhile, work by flattery and exclusion. “Those people are zealous for you, but not in a good way. Instead, they want to isolate you from us, so that you may be zealous for them.” Isolate is the strategy in one word: cut the congregation off from its founder, and loyalty to the cutters becomes the proof of devotion. Against their courtship Paul sets an image no recruiter would choose: “My children, for whom I am again in the pains of childbirth until Christ is formed in you.” Again, because he has already labored once to bring them to birth, and the false labor is now his to endure a second time. The letter's frustration spills into a wish: “how I wish I could be with you now and change my tone, because I am perplexed about you.” A letter cannot soften its voice mid-sentence. A man in the room could. The distance is part of the wound.

Now Paul takes the fight onto the teachers' own ground, the law itself, and reads them a story from it. “Tell me, you who want to be under the law, do you not understand what the law says? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and the other by the free woman.” The two births divide on one line: “His son by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, but his son by the free woman was born through the promise.” Ishmael is what Abraham could produce by arrangement; Isaac is what God produced by promise. Then Paul reads the household as a map of two covenants, and says so plainly: “These things serve as illustrations, for the women represent two covenants. One covenant is from Mount Sinai and bears children into slavery: This is Hagar.” Sinai, the law's mountain, is assigned to the slave woman, and its city is the earthly Jerusalem: Hagar “corresponds to the present-day Jerusalem, because she is in slavery with her children.” Against her stands the other mother: “But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother.” And Paul seals the reading with Isaiah's song to the barren woman: “Rejoice, O barren woman, who bears no children; break forth and cry aloud, you who have never travailed; because more are the children of the desolate woman than of her who has a husband.”

The application is then drawn tight around the Galatians' own necks, gently. “Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise.” Their standing in Abraham's house is Isaac's kind, born of promise, not of the flesh's arranging. And the old household tension has recurred on schedule: “the son born by the flesh persecuted the son born by the Spirit. It is the same now.” Genesis records Ishmael mocking; Paul reads the Galatian pressure campaign in the same line, the flesh's party harassing the promise's children in Abraham's own tent. Finally he lets Sarah's hard sentence in Genesis speak as the verdict, asking the question he asks of Scripture at his strongest moments: “But what does the Scripture say? ‘Expel the slave woman and her son, for the slave woman’s son will never share in the inheritance with the free woman’s son.’” The conclusion is one sentence, and it is addressed to people being recruited into slavery as if it were advancement: “Therefore, brothers, we are not children of the slave woman, but of the free woman.”

title: Stand Firm in Freedom
subtitle: Galatians 5:1–25
description: Freedom guarded from the flesh, and the Spirit’s ninefold fruit set against the flesh’s charge sheet.
paragraphs: The letter's long argument arrives at its command, and the command is a posture: “It is for freedom that Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery.” Then Paul prices the teachers' offer without flinching: “Take notice: I, Paul, tell you that if you let yourselves be circumcised, Christ will be of no value to you at all.” Not less value. None. The circumcision itself is not the catastrophe; the system it enrolls a man in is: “Again I testify to every man who gets himself circumcised that he is obligated to obey the whole law.” Part-law is not an option the law sells. Whoever takes the knife takes the entire code as his justification project, and the verdict on that project has already been given: “You who are trying to be justified by the law have been severed from Christ; you have fallen away from grace.” Severed and fallen are the vocabulary of loss, and Paul aims them at the most religious people in Galatia. Against the whole transaction stands one quiet sentence about the alternative: “But by faith we eagerly await through the Spirit the hope of righteousness.” And the only currency in Christ's economy: “For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value. What matters is faith expressing itself through love.”

He turns back to the race they had been running when he first knew them. “You were running so well. Who has obstructed you from obeying the truth?” Obstructed is a track word, a runner cut off mid-stride, and the new teaching is acquitted of any divine sponsorship: “Such persuasion does not come from the One who calls you.” Its danger is its smallness at the start: “A little leaven works through the whole batch of dough.” Paul is confident about the congregation and unsparing about its troubler: “The one who is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be.” One rumor about Paul himself gets answered in passing, the teachers' claim that he still preaches circumcision when it suits him: “if I am still preaching circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? In that case the offense of the cross has been abolished.” His scars are the rebuttal. Then, in the letter's most shocking sentence, he wishes the agitators would finish the logic of their own knife-work on themselves: “As for those who are agitating you, I wish they would proceed to emasculate themselves!” It is said once, in fury, at men turning surgery into a sacrament, and the letter moves on without apology or repetition.

Freedom, though, is not the absence of obligation, and Paul guards the word the moment he has won it. “For you, brothers, were called to freedom; but do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh. Rather, serve one another in love.” Serve is a slave's verb, deliberately chosen: the freed are to volunteer for the slavery that love imposes, the only kind left. The law the teachers want to impose piecemeal turns out to have a summary that the law-free life fulfills entire: “The entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’” And the Galatians' current quarrels show what fills a congregation instead when the flesh takes freedom's chair: “But if you keep on biting and devouring one another, watch out, or you will be consumed by one another.”

The alternative is a walk, and a war. “So I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh.” The conflict is structural, not occasional: “For the flesh craves what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh. They are opposed to each other, so that you do not do what you want.” Every believer in Galatia lives on that front line, and the front line is the proof of life, not of failure. One sentence closes the teachers' file for good: “But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.” Led, not driven; the Spirit's guidance and the law's guardianship are two different regimes, and a man cannot be enrolled in both.

The two regimes produce two harvests, and Paul lists them side by side. First the flesh's output, grouped like a charge sheet: “The acts of the flesh are obvious: sexual immorality, impurity, and debauchery; idolatry and sorcery; hatred, discord, jealousy, and rage; rivalries, divisions, factions, and envy; drunkenness, orgies, and the like.” Note how much of the list is social: the flesh's ripest fruit in this letter is a congregation at war with itself. The warning attached is not new information but a reminder: “those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.” Then the other list, and the grammar changes with the regime: not works of the flesh but fruit of the Spirit, singular, grown rather than manufactured: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” No law exists that these nine qualities break; the guardian's rulebook has no charge to file against them. The ground of it all is a finished execution and a daily step: “Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. Since we live by the Spirit, let us walk in step with the Spirit.”

title: Boast Only in the Cross
subtitle: Galatians 5:26–6:18
description: Burdens carried, seed sown, and the letter signed in large letters with one boast left standing.
paragraphs: The letter's last movement opens with the smallest of its warnings, aimed at the atmosphere of a congregation rather than its doctrine: “Let us not become conceited, provoking and envying one another.” Then the doctrine becomes a method for handling fallen people. “Brothers, if someone is caught in a trespass, you who are spiritual should restore him with a spirit of gentleness. But watch yourself, or you also may be tempted.” Restore is a bone-setter's word, the mending of a limb rather than the amputation of a member, and the spiritual are defined by gentleness under self-watch, not by severity. The burden economy follows: “Carry one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.” The law of Christ, in the letter that buried law-keeping as a way to God, is load-bearing love. Self-importance is the one load that helps no one: “If anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself.” So each believer is sent to his own audit rather than his neighbor's: “Each one should test his own work.” And two verses after the command to carry one another's burdens stands its apparent opposite, left unreconciled because both are true: “For each one should carry his own load.” The crushing weight is shared; the day's pack is personal. Galatia gets both sentences in one breath.

Then the farm law underneath the whole letter. The taught owe their teachers a share, “the one who receives instruction in the word must share in all good things with his instructor,” and above that arrangement stands the principle no arrangement escapes: “Do not be deceived: God is not to be mocked. Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return.” The two fields are named one last time: “The one who sows to please his flesh, from the flesh will reap destruction; but the one who sows to please the Spirit, from the Spirit will reap eternal life.” Sowing is slow and mostly invisible, which is why the next sentence exists: “Let us not grow weary in well-doing, for in due time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up.” The letter that began in astonishment at how quickly the Galatians were deserting ends by asking them to measure time by harvests rather than by moods. And the field for the sowing is as wide as the opportunity: “let us do good to everyone, and especially to the family of faith.”

Then the letter changes hands, literally. “See what large letters I am using to write to you with my own hand!” Paul takes the pen from his scribe for the closing, and the large letters are his signature and emphasis at once: what follows is underlined by the size of it. In his own hand he finally names the rival teachers' motives outright, the thing he has circled for six chapters: “Those who want to make a good impression outwardly are trying to compel you to be circumcised. They only do this to avoid persecution for the cross of Christ.” Impression and avoidance: their program is public relations with a knife. And their own obedience cannot bear the weight of their preaching: “For the circumcised do not even keep the law themselves, yet they want you to be circumcised that they may boast in your flesh.” Boast in your flesh: the Galatians' bodies are the trophy the campaign exists to collect.

Against that boast Paul sets his own, in the letter's climactic sentence: “But as for me, may I never boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.” The crucifixion runs both directions; the world is dead to Paul and Paul to the world, and the cross is the instrument of both deaths. What survives the double execution is then defined in the shortest creed in the letter: “For neither circumcision nor uncircumcision means anything. What counts is a new creation.” Not a repaired man, not a marked man, a new one. The blessing that follows is addressed to everyone who will walk by that rule: “Peace and mercy to all who walk by this rule, even to the Israel of God.”

The sign-off carries one scar and one grace note. “From now on let no one cause me trouble, for I bear on my body the marks of Jesus.” The marks are the literal record of the persecutions the teachers avoided, stripes and scars worn where a slave's brand would go, produced now as the final credential in a letter that began by defending credentials. And then, after six chapters of fire, the last line is a benediction, and the fire is simply gone from it: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.” The letter ends there, as letters do, without reporting what its readers answered. What the Galatian churches did with it, the letter does not say, and this telling will not invent it. The council in Jerusalem would take up the same question in its own time, and that story stands in Acts, where it belongs.
